correctness.rationale: The divisors of \(2^a p\) partition into the complementary pairs \((2^i,p2^{a-i})\). Subtracting an arbitrary omitted union from the exact divisor sum yields the reversible equation \(M-A_I=p(1+B_I)\). The cutoff is exhaustive because any \(a\ge12\) already makes \(2^a p>11776\). Fresh exact mask enumeration through \(a=11\) reproduced precisely the candidates \(6,28,496,352,8128,11776\), with 352 the unique one-pair nonperfect case and 11776 the first case whose unique representation has mask \(\{4,6\}\). Direct divisor-sum substitution verifies the omitted pairs and total.

originality.rationale: Wang–Zelinsky's full primary preprint was materially read. It defines strongly pseudoperfect representations, explicitly shows 156 can omit either one pair or two pairs, lists 352 with its unique omitted pair \((8,44)\), and proves a Mersenne-prime rigidity theorem for \(2^k p\). The earlier 2-near-perfect source classifies the one-omitted-pair \(2^k p\) subcase. Neither checked source states the arbitrary bit-mask criterion or identifies 11776 as the first \(2^a p\) case whose every representation genuinely needs multiple omitted complementary pairs. Resultary searches found no covering theorem.
residual_risks: An unindexed computation or note may contain the same 11776 observation.
The bit-mask criterion does not give a closed prime classification for all exponents.

final_claim: For \(n=2^a p\) with \(p\) an odd prime, strongly pseudoperfect representations are exactly governed by \(p=(2^{a+1}-1-A_I)/(1+B_I)\) for omitted complementary-pair masks \(I\); the first nonperfect such integer for which every representation needs at least two omitted pairs is \(11776=2^9\cdot23\), uniquely omitting \((16,736)\) and \((64,184)\).
scientific_limitations: An unindexed computation or note may contain the same 11776 observation.
The bit-mask criterion does not give a closed prime classification for all exponents.
The theorem is restricted to one odd-prime support \(2^a p\); it does not classify all strongly pseudoperfect numbers.
